cases.name: signed-json/unknown-member-is-signed-and-must-verify
cases.rule: Serialise and verify the document as received, unknown members included. Do not filter, do not normalise, do not reject.
cases.why: Adding a member is an explicitly compatible change. An implementation that rejects unknown members turns every future additive change into a network partition, and the partition appears on the day somebody else deploys.

cases.name: assertion/unknown-claim-is-ignored-not-rejected
cases.rule: Parse the claims leniently; verify the signature strictly over every byte received.
cases.why: The two halves pull in opposite directions and both are required. An implementation that is lenient in the parser and lenient in the verifier has no security; one that is strict in both has no forward compatibility.

cases.name: signed-json/key_id-is-outside-the-signed-bytes
cases.rule: `key_id` and `signature` are stripped before the bytes are formed. `key_id` is therefore unauthenticated routing metadata: use it to select a key, then let the signature decide.
cases.why: An implementation that includes `key_id` in the signed bytes produces documents no Telium server can verify, and the error it gets back says only 'invalid signature'.

note: Over-strictness is a compatibility bug with the same blast radius as under-strictness, and it is the one a careful implementer introduces on purpose.
time_dependent: Cases carrying `evaluate_at` are frozen so this file is byte-stable. Evaluate them with your clock set to that instant, or re-mint the artifact with the same offsets from your own now.
